payload.topWin: the restore rehearsal earned its existence twice in one session. It found that the backup captured no user-defined types — 38 tables that could never be created — and then, after that fix, found that the type references were unqualified and so resolved only in a database that already had `auth` in its search_path. **Neither defect was visible from inside the artifact.** Both were found by trying to use it, which is the entire argument for rehearsing a backup rather than counting its bytes.
payload.topGap: three of the rehearsal's own defects were mine, and each cost a two-hour run to surface — the wrong target image, an authentication failure mistaken for a corrupt archive, and a readiness check that returned true during an init phase. The harness was less trustworthy than its subject for most of the session, and a rehearsal that fails for reasons unrelated to the backup is worse than no rehearsal because it looks exactly like a corrupt archive.

payload.headline: 13 of 78 gates ran from no automated entry point; the ratchet marked DONE at S309 had never once executed
payload.pattern: A locus checker asks whether every blocking gate is ALSO enforced server-side, so it can only ask that of gates already in a hook. It is structurally blind to a gate in no hook at all.
payload.solution: Measure reachability transitively from real entry points, reading edges from CODE not comments; a gate reachable only from another dead gate is equally dead; absence renders UNMEASURED, never green.

payload.pattern: A canonical-asset sync that overwrites a whole file silently reverts locally-shipped contracts inside it, and the resulting suite red can sit undiagnosed for days
payload.solution: Two layers. (1) The existing outbound guard compares NAMED EXPORTS only, so any contract expressed as an option parameter, call site, or gating expression is invisible to it - widen it, or accept that it is only half a guard. (2) Each downstream repo declares an inbound manifest (docs/SYNC_PROTECTED_CONTRACTS.json) naming the contract at whatever granularity it actually exists, asserted by a test-suite checker that is itself proved against the real historical clobber commit rather than against a lookalike fixture. Measured live in analytica: validate-brief-format.mjs lost criticalTruncation and checkSourceFingerprint to a sync on 2026-08-24, was restored 2026-08-26, and lost both again on 2026-09-01; the suite then sat red for 8 days while the startup brief displayed Tests-red every session. Requesting the two contracts be carried in the canonical studio-ops copy so the manifest entries can retire.

payload.topWin: the executor earned its existence on its first run, in both directions at once. `rescore-ignis --stale` **exited 1 and CLEARED its probe**; `rotate-ledgers --apply` **exited 0 and moved twin-history 5.2MB to 5.1MB with the probe still red**. Neither fact is visible from an exit code, and the second is a broken promise that had been reading as a clean run for two sessions. A gate that records *what changed about the thing the remedy claimed to fix* is worth more than one that records whether a command succeeded — and this one found the distinction the day it was switched on.
payload.topGap: I keep building instruments whose own path I have not watched execute. The serial-retry fix went into `run-doctor.mjs`, the next full run had a quiet host, `0/219 probes could not run`, and the recovery path never ran — I would have shipped it on the strength of two probes going green for an unrelated reason. Extracting it and driving it directly was the fix, but the reflex that needed correcting is the one that matters: **a surrounding number turning green is not evidence that my change is what turned it.** The same reflex is why the `tests` probe is still red at session end — the failing assertion is fixed and the guard is 47/47 standalone, and I have no measured full-suite number to put behind that.
